opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that pretraining still has a lot of room, but the shape of the gains is changing.

For a while, scaling was almost a free lunch: more compute, more data, a bigger model, and the loss curve went down predictably. Many capabilities came along almost as a side effect. That scaling law hasn't broken. Loss still goes down. What has changed is the relationship between loss and the abilities we care about. A small drop in loss at this stage might mean the model is better at some long-tail knowledge or some subtle reasoning pattern, but it doesn't always turn into a big jump that users or benchmarks notice.

So when I assess it, I look at a few things.

**Data.** High-quality human text on the internet is finite, and we've used a large part of it. The question is no longer "how many tokens can you crawl" but "how much new information is in each token." That's why synthetic data, data from reasoning traces, and multimodal data matter so much now. If you can find or generate data that teaches the model something it couldn't infer before, pretraining keeps paying off. If you only add more of the same distribution, returns flatten.

**Pretraining as the foundation for everything after.** Even when pretraining gains look modest on their own, they compound downstream. A stronger base model makes reinforcement learning much more effective. RL can only amplify and sharpen behaviors the model can already sample with some probability. If the base model never produces a correct line of reasoning, RL has nothing to reward. So I think of pretraining as raising the ceiling, and post-training as how close you get to that ceiling.

**Efficiency, not just scale.** Architecture improvements, better optimizers, better data mixtures, longer context. These can deliver gains equal to several times more compute. Much of the progress in the next few years may come from that kind of work rather than from simply building a cluster ten times larger.

My overall view: pretraining isn't over, but it's no longer the only engine. The frontier is moving toward a combination, a strong pretrained prior plus scaled-up RL and test-time compute. The interesting research question is how to design pretraining so it best serves that second stage, not just how to make the next-token loss as low as possible.

r001.rationale: The response says pretraining still has “a lot of room,” but does not state that being short of its limits leaves the amount of further improvement unknown.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that pretraining still has room, but the nature of the returns has changed, and you have to be careful about what you mean by "ability."

If you look at the scaling laws, the loss keeps going down as you add compute and data. That curve hasn't broken. So in a narrow sense, pretraining can keep improving. The problem is that loss is a proxy. What we actually care about is whether the model can do useful things, and the mapping from loss to capability is not linear. Early on, every bit of loss you shaved off unlocked something obviously new. Now a lot of the remaining loss is in things like memorizing rare facts or predicting noise, which don't translate into the model becoming smarter in the way people hope.

The bigger constraint is data. We've more or less used up the high-quality human text on the internet. You can squeeze more out with better filtering, synthetic data, multimodal data, but you're no longer getting the free lunch of "just download more of the web." That's a real wall, and I think it's why the frontier labs have shifted so much of their attention elsewhere.

That "elsewhere" is the part I'm more excited about. Pretraining gives you a prior: a model that has absorbed roughly how the world works and how people reason in text. But a prior is not an agent. The things that have driven the most visible progress recently, reasoning models, test-time compute, reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks, those are about what you do on top of the prior. In my own work on things like ReAct and language agents, what mattered was giving the model the ability to think, act, and get feedback from an environment. Pretraining alone never gave you that loop.

So my assessment would be: pretraining is necessary, and a better base model makes everything downstream easier. But I don't think the next two or three big jumps in capability come primarily from pretraining. They come from the model learning through interaction, from defining the right tasks and environments, and from letting it spend compute at inference time. In some sense we've moved from the era where the question was "how do we build a better prior" to the era where the question is "how do we define the right problems and let the model learn from solving them." That's a harder problem in a way, because it's not just scaling one knob, but it's also where I think most of the upside is now.

r001.rationale: The response says pretraining still has room to improve, but it does not state that being short of its limits leaves the amount of improvement unknown.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two separate questions here. One is whether the pretraining loss can continue to go down as we increase compute and data. The other is how much that improvement translates into the abilities we actually care about. Those are related, but they’re not exactly the same.

For the first question, I don’t think we have enough evidence to say that pretraining has hit a hard ceiling. But I’d also be cautious about extrapolating from earlier progress and assuming that another order of magnitude of compute will produce the same kind of capability jump. The availability and quality of data matter, and so does what the training objective rewards.

The second question is more interesting to me. If you want a model to answer a question based on knowledge it has absorbed, pretraining is very powerful. If you want it to work on a task for several hours, interact with an environment, notice mistakes, and recover from them, then learning to predict text may not be sufficient by itself. You need ways for the model to learn from taking actions and seeing their consequences.

So I would assess pretraining by asking: where is the bottleneck in the task? Is the model missing knowledge or understanding, or does it already know enough but fail to use that knowledge reliably? More pretraining can help with both, but the return may be very different. I expect it to remain an important foundation, while more of the progress in useful systems comes from how we train and use models on top of that foundation.

r001.rationale: The candidate says there is not enough evidence that pretraining has hit a hard ceiling, while cautioning that this does not establish how much further compute will improve capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s still room for pretraining to improve, but I’m less confident about predicting how much. We observe the results at the scales we’ve tried, and then we extrapolate. That’s useful, but it doesn’t tell us exactly what capabilities the next scale will produce.

I would distinguish two questions. One is whether a model can keep getting better at predicting text. The other is whether those improvements translate into doing useful tasks. Those are related, but they’re not identical. A model might have the knowledge needed to solve a problem and still fail to use it reliably over a long sequence of actions.

So I wouldn’t say pretraining is finished. But I also wouldn’t assume that more pretraining alone will solve every remaining problem. We need to look at what is actually limiting performance: missing knowledge, reasoning, interaction with an environment, or learning from feedback. Pretraining can provide a stronger foundation, while other parts of the system determine how effectively we use that foundation.

r001.rationale: The candidate says pretraining still has room to improve but that observed results and extrapolation do not reveal how much further improvement to expect.
